sentences.text: Neovenator was a mid-sized, lightly built carcharodontosaurid that likely measured around 7 meters in length and weighed 1 metric ton, though one possibly referable specimen suggests a size of 10 meters.
The skull of this predator measures 70 cm in length, and the holotype specimen preserves six cervical vertebrae and twelve dorsal vertebrae.
The holotype preserves nearly complete left scapula and coracoid bones, but the forelimbs are not known.
Bite marks on a Mantellisaurus fossil provide direct evidence that Neovenator preyed on this iguanodontid dinosaur.
Teeth associated with the type specimen possess characteristic enamel wrinkles but differ in their precise pattern from other carcharodontosaur teeth.
The holotype specimen exhibited significant pathology, including fused caudal vertebrae, healed gastralia fractures, a scapula fracture, regrown gastralium, and osteophytes on foot bones.
The first remains of Neovenator were discovered in the summer of 1978 after a storm-induced collapse at Grange Chine.
The genus Neovenator and its type species, Neovenator salerii, were named in 1996 by Steve Hutt, David Martill, and Michael Barker.
The holotype was found in a plant debris bed sandwiched between sandstone and mudstone layers.
Researchers noted in 2001 that Neovenator likely hunted via ambush due to limb proportions unsuited for high speeds.
Researchers speculated that Neovenator may have hunted large prey in groups, similar to crocodilians and Komodo dragons.

Researchers suggested Neovenator possessed integumentary sensory organs on its snout based on neurovascular structures found in the skull, and because Neovenator was terrestrial, researchers assume these organs were used for sensing pressure, temperature, and controlling jaw pressure rather than finding food in water.
Researchers hypothesize Neovenator may have used sensory organs for courtship and sensing nest conditions.

The holotype specimen exhibited significant pathology similar to that seen in Allosaurus, including fused caudal vertebrae, healed gastralia fractures, a scapula fracture, regrown gastralium, and osteophytes on foot bones.
A position within the clade Carcharodontosauria was first suggested in 1998 and supported by comparative morphology and phylogenetic analyses.
In 2010, Neovenator was assigned to its own family, Neovenatoridae.

Researchers suggested in 1996 that Neovenator was closely related to Allosaurus and possibly a member of the family Allosauridae, and a 2000 phylogenetic analysis by Thomas R. Holtz Jr. recovered Neovenator as the sister taxon to Allosaurus.
Neovenator belongs to the parent group Neovenatoridae.
Neovenator lived during the Barremian stage of the Early Cretaceous, between 125.77 and 121.4 million years ago.
Definite Neovenator remains are from the Barremian-age Wessex Formation of the Isle of Wight, while teeth from the Berriasian-age Angeac-Charente bone bed in France may also belong to the genus.
The Wessex Formation environment was a floodplain intersected by river and lake deposits.

Evidence of burned plant material suggests the environment experienced frequent wildfires that limited gymnosperm growth, and the flora consisted mainly of low-lying pteridophytes with occasional conifers, cycads, and the tree fern Tempskya.

The taxonomic position of Neovenator remains a subject of debate; Fernando Novas et al. (2013) placed Neovenator at the base of Carcharodontosauridae in a polytomy with Eocarcharia and Concavenator, while researchers suggest that the snout of Neovenator was highly vascularized or innervated.
